newsitem.title: JAPAN: INTERVIEW - NTT sees firms eager for its intl move.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - NTT sees firms eager for its intl move.

text.p: Japanese telecoms titan NTT, which will move into international business as early as August, says it is receiving a flood of inquiries from companies about its proposed "one-stop" service.

"We have received a surprisingly large number of inquiries, and talks have already begun with quite a few of the world's big names, including foreign firms," NTT vice president Tatsuo Kawasaki told Reuters in an interview.

Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp, the world's biggest telecoms firm with eight trillion yen in group sales, is expected to get the go-ahead to enter the international arena this summer after parliament revises the law governing its business.
Kawasaki said NTT would set up a new subsidiary around August to launch an NTT-brand "one-stop" service for data communications.
The "one-stop" service allows multinationals to pay bills to a single telecoms supplier, which operates and manages seamless global communications networks for clients.

It will be in competition with three main global alliances: Concert, a tie-up of British Telecommunications Plc and MCI Communications Corp of the United States; Global One, consisting of Deutsche Telekom, France Telecom and Sprint of the United States; and WorldPartners, a loose group assembled by U.S. giant AT&T.
NTT's targets are Japanese multinationals operating in Europe and America and foreign firms with plans to build new networks into Asia.
"To some Japanese customers, NTT's strong brand name, large corporate size and funds appear to be attractive," said Kawasaki, who is in charge of NTT's global network project.

Rivals say NTT has already posted 800 employees around the globe for its international business, invested in foreign networks and offered systems integration services, but Kawasaki declined to give details.
NTT has earmarked 100 billion yen for overseas investment in 1997/98.

NTT will initially lease cables from local operators but will build its own networks in the second stage in areas where demand is large, Kawasaki said. It is also investigating the possible use of communications satellites, he said.

"We can offer such a global service on our own, to some extent, without linking up with one particular global telecoms consortium," he said, reiterating NTT's stance that it would not form an exclusive tie-up with one telecoms group.
"We hope to keep a neutral position so that we can offer our customers flexible services that best meet their demands," he said.
On the U.S. government's decision to delay granting NTT an international licence, Kawasaki said it is a big headache that could affect its whole international business.
"The biggest demand certainly lies in communications between Japan and the United States," he said, adding that the licence is vital for its service.

The U.S. Federal Communications Commission decided in March to delay granting NTT and Japanese international carrier Kokusai Denshin Denwa Co U.S. international phone licences, citing insufficient international procurement by NTT.

If the delay is prolonged, NTT will connect its lines with those of U.S. carriers to include the U.S. market in its global service. "But that would be far from our initial objective of offering a one-stop service," Kawasaki said.
